newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Doctors try to reduce death toll from childbirth.
newsitem.headline: Doctors try to reduce death toll from childbirth.

text.p: Doctors and medical specialists from 75 countries start a week-long conference on Monday to put the spotlight on the agony of one million women a year who die in childbirth.
They are gathering in Morocco's red-walled city of Marrakesh to hold the first world congress on maternal mortality and to try to bring down the death toll.

Congress spokesman Badr Tazi told Reuters: "The main objective is to examine in detail the maternal mortality issue in the developing world and draw up an active plan of support for areas which lack basic health infrastructure."
Tazi, a doctor who heads a public hospital in the Moroccan town of Temara, said maternal mortality mainly in Africa was "a real tragedy which needs an urgent solution".

"An average 330 women out of 100,000 women die at childbirth annually in Morocco," he said, according to latest figures. But this remained far below other African countries where the rate fluctuates between 800 to 1,000 every year.
The equivalent figure in Scandinavian countries is 10 to 15 women, he added.
Abderrahim Baroudi, Moroccan professor and paediatrician, said: "Most of the deaths are from obstetric causes such as haemorrhage, and an unsafe childbirth environment."
In remote areas, authorities needed "to set up a minimum infrastructure and train local people in order to identify risky pregnancy and avoid the mother's death," he said.
Baroudi said specialists knew the problems and solutions but attention had not been focused on the tragedy.

"From my point of view, the Marrakesh meeting should be a launching pad for a worldwide campaign to alert public opinion on risks surrounding childbirth and the minimum care women need to avoid disaster," Baroudi added.
UNICEF, the U.N. Children's Fund, whose representatives will attend the Marrakesh conference, estimated in its annual report nearly 600,000 deaths in childbirth in 1990.
An international group of physicians, the World Society on Labor and Delivery, says one million women die each year in childbirth, most of them in Africa and southern Asia.

Dr Daniel Weinstein, president of the society, said last month he had had trouble raising the more than $500,000 needed for the congress. He said only Switzerland and Norway had responded to an appeal for funds.
The five-day congress has registered 750 delegates so far, officials said.
"One reason that the world is quiet is that we don't hear any noise from Africa, from Asia. They are dying in silence. And the silence has put the world to sleep," Weinstein said.
